title: Scheduled Task/Job: Systemd Timers
summary: This sub-technique covers recurring execution through systemd timers, the modern alternative to cron on Linux distributions that use systemd as their service manager. A timer is a unit file whose name ends in .timer, and it does not contain the command itself: it activates a service unit of the same base name, so a unit pair of a timer and a service is really two files, often installed together by whoever wants the work to run. Timers support both monotonic schedules, measured from an event such as boot or the last run, and calendar schedules, and they can be set persistent so a missed run happens after the machine comes back up. Units can be placed in system-wide directories for privileged work or in a per-user directory for work that runs only in that user's session, and they can be created or started over a remote connection with the systemctl utility. The artefacts are therefore file-based and journal-based: unit files appearing outside package management, a daemon reload followed by an enable or start, and journal entries showing the service repeatedly started with no interactive session behind it.

beginner.definition: Systemd is the part of many Linux systems that starts and manages background services. A timer is a small file that tells systemd to start a service on a schedule. This sub-technique is when an attacker installs a timer so their program runs again and again. It is part of the Scheduled Task/Job parent, and it is the modern replacement for cron on many systems.
beginner.whyItMatters: Timers are newer than cron, so fewer checklists mention them and fewer people know where they live. A privileged timer can keep root access alive across reboots, and a per-user timer keeps access inside one account. Because the timer and the service are separate files, an analyst may miss the schedule. They may read only the service file. Learned skill here closes a common blind spot.
howItWorks: The attacker writes a service unit that names the program to run. Then they write a timer unit with the same base name.
The timer says when to act. It can use a calendar time, or a delay measured from boot or the previous run.
They place the files in a system directory for root level work, or in a user directory for one account.
They ask systemd to reload its configuration, then enable the timer so it also survives a reboot.
Systemd starts the matching service whenever the timer elapses, with no login session involved.
The admin can also do this remotely over a secure shell connection using the systemctl utility.
beginner.example: Picture an apartment building with a printed cleaning rota pinned in the lobby. The rota does not name a cleaner directly; it points to a numbered instruction card kept in a drawer. Someone pins up a new rota line and adds a matching card. The cleaner follows the card every Sunday at dawn, exactly as instructed. If you only read the cards, nothing looks wrong, because the strange part is the rota entry itself.
takeaways: A timer and its service come as a pair, so always read both files.
Unit files in privileged paths give lasting root level access.
A reload followed by an enable or start is a strong clue in the system journal.

objectives: Explain the relationship between a timer unit and the service unit it activates.
Describe the difference between calendar timers and timers measured from an event.
Identify where privileged and per-user unit files are stored and what each location implies.
Recognise the journal and file artefacts left when a timer is installed and enabled.
Explain how systemd timers differ from cron entries in structure and in detection.
